claims.claim: Martinson's 1974 article was based on 231 studies selected from the post-World-War-II to 1967 evaluation literature for a New York State survey, drawn from a roughly 1,400-page unpublished manuscript, and its summary sentence was that with few and isolated exceptions the rehabilitative efforts reported so far had had no appreciable effect on recidivism.

Before stating that conclusion, Martinson warned that studies using the term recidivism rate were often measuring different things - arrest rates, parole violation rates, or success measures such as favorable discharge - and that those measures do not correlate highly; near the end of the article he wrote that it was just possible some treatment programs were working but the research was too poor to detect it, and that unmeasured deterrence might be doing work.

In 1979, in the Hofstra Law Review, Martinson withdrew the 1974 conclusion and his characterization of treatment as impotent, and reported from a larger survey of 555 studies that treatment programs can be beneficial, neutral, or detrimental depending on the conditions under which they are delivered.

The risk-need-responsivity model, first formalized in 1990 by Andrews, Bonta and Hoge, states three principles: match the level of service to risk of reoffending, assess and target criminogenic needs, and deliver treatment using cognitive social learning methods tailored to the individual's learning style, motivation, abilities and strengths.

Bonta and Andrews identify seven dynamic major risk/need factors - antisocial personality pattern, procriminal attitudes, social supports for crime, substance abuse, family/marital relationships, school/work, and prosocial recreational activities - which together with static criminal history make up the central eight.

Bonta and Andrews report the following average recidivism differences: about 10 percent when treatment is delivered to higher-risk cases against about 3 percent for lower-risk cases across 374 tests of the risk principle; about 19 percent for adherence to the need principle, with about a 1 percent increase when non-criminogenic needs are targeted; about 23 percent for adherence to general responsivity; and about 17 percent in residential or custodial settings and 35 percent in community settings when all three principles are adhered to, with interventions adhering to none associated with increased recidivism.

Bonta and Andrews report that the effectiveness of treatment delivered in real-world correctional settings is about half the effect of the experimental demonstration program, and that staff assessment accuracy drifts over time, which is why program integrity and implementation quality are treated as part of the intervention.

States and the Federal Bureau of Prisons reported 453,242 releases of sentenced prisoners in 2023 - 408,521 from state systems and 44,721 from the federal system - against 472,300 admissions, and about 70 percent of prison releases in both 2022 and 2023 were conditional on community supervision or other requirements.

The BJS prison release count covers prisoners sentenced to more than one year and excludes local jails, where turnover is far higher: people admitted to local jails from July 2022 to June 2023 spent an average of 32 days in custody before release.

NIJ defines recidivism as a person's relapse into criminal behavior after sanction or intervention and notes that it is typically measured by criminal acts resulting in rearrest, reconviction, or return to incarceration over a stated follow-up period, so definitions vary across studies.

Among state prisoners released in 30 states in 2005, BJS reported that 68 percent were arrested within 3 years, 79 percent within 6 years, and 83 percent within 9 years, across a cohort of 401,288 released prisoners.
Among prisoners released in 34 states in 2012, BJS reported that 62 percent were arrested within 3 years and 71 percent within 5 years, and that 46 percent returned to prison within 5 years.

Among prisoners released in 24 states in 2008 and followed ten years, BJS reported that 66 percent were arrested within 3 years and 82 percent within 10 years, while 61 percent returned to prison within 10 years for a parole or probation violation or a new sentence, and the annual arrest percentage fell from 43 percent in year one to 22 percent in year ten.

NIJ's CrimeSolutions rates the practice Adult Reentry Programs as Promising for reducing recidivism: Ndrecka's meta-analysis of 53 studies and 289,125 participants found a statistically significant effect of r = .06, which the profile translates as a 47 percent recidivism rate for participants against 53 percent for comparisons, while Berghuis's meta-analysis of randomized trials with adult male samples found no statistically significant effect on rearrest.

CrimeSolutions rates the practice Rehabilitation Programs for Adults Convicted of a Crime as Promising based on Lipsey's 2019 meta-analysis of 801 studies, and reports that structured or psychoeducational group work, cognitive behavioral components, counseling, and drug or other specialized courts were associated with statistically significant recidivism reductions while work-related, academic, supportive residential, intensive supervision, multimodal, and restorative interventions were not.

An Oklahoma juvenile reentry program funded under the Second Chance Act is rated Ineffective by CrimeSolutions after a quasi-experimental evaluation found no statistically significant difference in reconviction at 18 months post-release between participants and comparisons.

RAND's 2013 meta-analysis for the Bureau of Justice Assistance found that participants in correctional education had 43 percent lower odds of recidivating than nonparticipants, which the authors translate into a 13 percentage-point reduction in risk, that the result was stable when lower-quality studies were included, and that high school or GED participants had 30 percent lower odds.

RAND reported weaker employment findings: 13 percent higher odds of postrelease employment overall, but with only one study in the higher-quality category, so the authors state they are limited in their ability to detect a statistically significant difference; vocational participants showed 28 percent higher odds and academic participants 8 percent, with no statistically significant difference between the two.

The Second Chance Act of 2007, Public Law 110-199, was approved April 9, 2008, authorizes adult and juvenile offender reentry demonstration projects, state, tribal and local reentry courts, mentoring and transitional service grants, and substance-abuse programming, and its purposes are codified at 34 U.S.C. 60501; several of its sections were amended by the First Step Act of 2018, Public Law 115-391.

Federal Medicaid law excludes payment for care or services for an individual who is an inmate of a public institution, except as a patient in a medical institution, which is why re-establishing health coverage is a discrete task at release.

California requires its Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles to ensure that eligible people released from state prison obtain a valid California identification card, and directs the department to facilitate obtaining the underlying documentation; the section was amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 482.

Housing Choice Voucher regulations require a public housing agency to deny admission where a household member is subject to a lifetime state sex-offender registration requirement or has been convicted of manufacturing methamphetamine on the premises of federally assisted housing, and permit denial on other criminal-history grounds.

EEOC enforcement guidance treats criminal-record screens as subject to Title VII disparate-impact analysis, treats exclusion based on an arrest alone as not job related and consistent with business necessity, and assesses conviction-based exclusions against the nature and gravity of the offense, time elapsed, and the nature of the job.

Collateral consequences of conviction are numerous and catalogued jurisdiction by jurisdiction; the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, compiling the National Inventory of Collateral Consequences of Conviction as of February 2019, counted approximately 44,631 of them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Martinson concluded that nothing works.
positions: The widely repeated version: a 1974 review established that rehabilitation is ineffective.

The 1974 text: a summary that reported no appreciable effect, explicitly hedged by warnings that recidivism measures differ, that follow-up periods rarely extend past legal supervision, that experiments were unreplicated, and that the research might be too weak to detect real effects.
The 1979 text: Martinson withdraws the conclusion and reports that programs are beneficial, neutral, or detrimental depending on delivery conditions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports all three, cites the 1974 phrase in quotation marks with attribution, and states plainly that the slogan misrepresents both articles. It does not use Martinson as authority for any claim about whether rehabilitation works today.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The Adult Reentry Programs practice profile reports two meta-analyses with divergent results.
positions: Ndrecka (2014), 53 studies, statistically significant r = .06 reduction in recidivism.
Berghuis (2018), randomized trials with adult male samples only, no statistically significant effect on rearrest.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported in the lesson. The profile's narrative describes eight randomized controlled trials while its meta-analysis snapshot table lists nine studies for that analysis; because the discrepancy is internal to the source, the lesson describes the analysis as limited to randomized trials of adult male samples and does not state a study count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to state the RAND correctional education result.
positions: About a 13 percentage-point reduction in the risk of recidivating.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are RAND's own figures for the same result, and the lesson gives both while naming them as different quantities. The translation was checked arithmetically: an odds ratio of 0.57 applied to a 50 percent comparison rate yields about 36.3 percent, a 13.7 percentage-point difference, consistent with RAND's stated 13 points.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether correctional education causes the recidivism reduction RAND reports.
positions: The pooled association is large and stable across study quality strata.

Studies rating 2 or higher on the Maryland Scientific Methods Scale were eligible, so non-randomized comparisons of participants to nonparticipants qualified, and RAND itself reports methodological weaknesses, unmeasured dosage, and an inability to disentangle program types.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the finding as RAND states it, notes the stability across quality strata, states that non-randomized designs were eligible under the Maryland Scientific Methods Scale threshold RAND used, and says explicitly that selection into programs remains a live threat.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about rehabilitation or reentry at all; its body text was placeholder prose about defining a concept and applying it to a scenario, with no reference to Martinson, recidivism measurement, risk-need-responsivity, release volumes, or any statute.

The draft's vocabulary defined the topic title circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson' and offered generic entries for context, evidence, and application.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy (a label on a toolbox drawer, a map legend) carried no subject content and had no statement of where the analogy breaks down.
The draft's quick-check items tested nothing about the topic and offered three options rather than four.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content.
Set estimated minutes from 8 to 13 to match a topic that carries a historiographical argument, a measurement framework, quantitative findings, and a legal barriers section.

Wrote the Martinson material from both primary articles rather than from the secondary slogan, including the 1979 withdrawal, which is the single most common error in student and popular writing on this topic.
Made the rearrest/reconviction/return-to-prison distinction the organizing methodological point, with a worked example that shows the same BJS cohort producing 82 percent and 61 percent.
Dated every quantitative figure and named its population, including the 2023 release counts and the three BJS recidivism cohorts.

Reported CrimeSolutions ratings at the strength the clearinghouse assigned, including the null results inside otherwise Promising profiles and an Ineffective Second Chance Act-funded program, rather than presenting reentry programming as established.
Stated the RAND finding as lower odds and as a percentage-point risk difference, and reported the weaker employment result with the authors' own caveat about a single high-quality study.
Kept collateral consequences doctrine, supervision and revocation mechanics, and institutional typology out of scope, cross-referencing the topics that own them.
Added an explicit educational-material statement in provenance and in the Why This Matters section, took no policy position, and gave no legal, benefits, or medical advice.
rightsIssues: Martinson's 1974 Public Interest article and 1979 Hofstra Law Review article are under copyright. Both were read in full for research; only a five-word phrase from the 1974 article is quoted, in quotation marks and attributed. No other wording is reproduced.
The Public Safety Canada report is Crown copyright with no reuse licence stated on the document; treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and paraphrased.
RAND documents carry an explicit notice restricting reproduction and reuse; treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and paraphrased. Findings and numbers are facts and are reported as such with attribution.

BJS, NIJ and CrimeSolutions pages are federal works but their sites do not state a blanket reuse licence for all content, and existing registry records for BJS and CrimeSolutions classify them REFERENCE_ONLY; that classification is carried forward here for consistency.
NICCC states no reuse licence and its own disclaimer says the site is educational and not legal advice; used for scope only.
U.S. statutes, the public law text on govinfo, federal regulations, the EEOC guidance, the USCCR report, and California statutory text are edicts of government or federal works and are public domain.
